talks.title: Ali - Dev Ally
talks.teaser: Security researchers investigate Ali - Dev Ally and analyze defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
Overview: Ali presents at BalCCon on DevAlly, sharing a year of hands-on experiments testing Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) solutions across the application security ecosystem.

Key Topics: Shifting left in the SDLC; static versus dynamic analysis integration; RASP deployment challenges; Ali's upcoming book on application security; and the principle of sharing knowledge in the security community.

Technical Details: As application security lead at Canon, Ali evaluated multiple RASP solutions over a year, comparing their effectiveness within the broader AppSec toolchain including SAST, DAST, and penetration testing workflows.

Takeaways: RASP is one layer in a comprehensive AppSec program, not a silver bullet. Practitioners should test solutions hands-on and integrate them thoughtfully into existing SDLC processes.

talks.title: Brian - Darknet Data Deluge - A Script Kiddies Guide to Efficient Leak Analysis
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Brian - Darknet Data Deluge - A Script Kiddies Guide to Efficient Leak Analysis.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Swiss cyber security specialist Brian presents a tactical guide to discovering, acquiring, and analyzing ransomware leaks and darknet data dumps at BalcCon. Drawing on experiences investigating real-world cyber extortion campaigns, Brian outlines the technical challenges of downloading multi-gigabyte and terabyte-scale archives over high-latency anonymity networks. He details custom automation pipelines built to scrape ransomware leak portals, bypass anti-bot protections, and systematically triage unstructured leak repositories to identify compromised corporate credentials and partner data.

Key Topics:
- Monitoring ransomware leak portals across cybercriminal gangs (Play, LockBit, 8Base) and darknet forums
- Optimizing Tor connectivity and throughput using create_torrc and containerized proxies
- Automating darknet scraping and bypassing anti-DDoS CAPTCHAs using Playwright and AI models
- Tactical triage and forensic analysis of unstructured leak archives (user homes, cloud migrations, password files)

Technical Details:
Brian outlines the operational landscape of darknet data dumps, spanning structured database breaches (such as NATO database sales on BreachForums or 440 GB Fortinet leaks in public S3 buckets) to massive unstructured dumps published by double-extortion ransomware groups. Because darknet onion services frequently suffer from extreme latency, low bandwidth, and single-source bottlenecks—sometimes requiring up to 20 days to download a single terabyte-scale leak—Brian developed custom tooling to optimize acquisition. To accelerate throughput, he utilizes create_torrc to query public node telemetry, filtering Tor routing tables to include only the 1,000 fastest relays situated within his local country, trading anonymity for download speed. He encapsulates this optimized Tor daemon within Docker containers to serve as an HTTP/SOCKS proxy for headless curl and Python clients.

When ransomware groups implement JavaScript queuing systems, WebSockets, or CAPTCHA challenges to block automated scrapers (observed on portals like Play and Cloak), simple HTTP scraping fails. To overcome this, Brian implemented browser automation using Playwright and Chromium. To bypass CAPTCHAs, he trained a custom machine learning model on an hour of manually labeled CAPTCHA samples, allowing headless browsers to solve image challenges, navigate directory listings, and log webpage changes every 15 minutes via his "Play Watcher" daemon. This scraper detected when broken archive files were re-uploaded, allowing rapid re-fetching. For high-volume file transfers, he leverages tools like Aria2c, JDownloader with multi-threaded connection chunking, or seedboxes and services like Real-Debrid for clearnet torrent magnets.

For post-acquisition analysis, Brian examines real-world case studies including NullBulge's 1.22 TB leak of Disney Slack messages (retrieved via Web Archive copies of suspended clearnet sites and torrent seedboxes) and the Play ransomware leak targeting Swiss software provider Xplain. To efficiently triage unstructured dumps, Brian recommends inspecting user home directories (Desktop, Downloads) where employees store unencrypted password.txt files and unmanaged database backups from migrations. He also demonstrates search methodologies: searching for internal company codenames, business partner domains, and checking adjacent files—such as finding plaintext passwords written in plain text files directly alongside "unbreakable" encrypted zip archives.

Key Takeaways:
Defensive organizations and intelligence teams must actively monitor darknet ransomware portals to detect supply chain compromises and credential exposures before third-party incidents are publicly acknowledged. Accelerating leak ingestion requires specialized infrastructure: curated Tor routing configurations, multi-connection download managers, and headless browser automation with CAPTCHA-solving capabilities. Finally, enterprises must enforce automated endpoint hygiene to prevent staff from storing sensitive credentials, database exports, and migration dumps in personal desktop and download folders.

talks.title: cluosh - Here be Dragons
talks.teaser: Ghidra Decompiler API Adventures details cluosh - Here be Dragons.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Security researcher cluosh presents an in-depth reverse engineering analysis of Ghidra's C++ decompiler architecture and the SLEIGH processor specification engine at BalcCon. The speaker details the decoupling between Ghidra's Java-based GUI and its standalone C++ native binaries, explaining the XML-based inter-process communication mechanisms used during analysis. Through practical demonstrations, cluosh illustrates how to directly interface with Ghidra's native libraries (sleigh, libdecomp) to build custom, high-speed command-line disassemblers and decompilers without invoking the Java runtime.

Key Topics:
- Ghidra dual architecture: Java front-end GUI and loaders versus C++ native decompiler (decompile, sleigh)
- SLEIGH processor specification language, .sla bytecode files, and .pspec context variables
- Low-level P-code intermediate representation: varnodes, address spaces, and Static Single Assignment (SSA) form
- Building standalone native reverse engineering utilities using libdecomp, AssemblyEmit, and PcodeEmit

Technical Details:
cluosh explains that Ghidra isolates its heavy lifting in C++ native binaries (decompile / decompile.exe and sleigh) running in separate processes, deliberately avoiding the Java Native Interface (JNI) so that decompiler segmentation faults do not crash the main Java application. Communication between the Java GUI and native back-end occurs over pipes using serialized XML streams. Architecture support is driven by SLEIGH, a domain-specific processor specification language compiled into binary .sla files (located under Ghidra/Processors/<arch>/data/languages/). When loading architectures like x86 or RISC-V, SLEIGH relies on processor specification (.pspec) files to establish hardware context variables, such as address size (addrsize) or execution mode flags (e.g., 16-bit, 32-bit, or 64-bit decoding).

SLEIGH lifts machine instructions into P-code, an intermediate representation composed of P-code operations (PcodeOp) acting upon varnodes (Varnode). Varnodes represent storage locations defined by an address space (AddressSpace, such as memory, register, stack, or constant) and an offset. During decompilation, raw low-level P-code is transformed into High P-code structured in Static Single Assignment (SSA) form, introducing synthetic operations like MULTIEQUAL (phi-nodes) and INDIRECT to merge divergent execution paths and track memory aliases. The decompiler aggressively eliminates dead code; cluosh cautions that incorrect function prototypes or missing volatile annotations on memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) regions—such as those encountered when reverse engineering the BalcCon hardware badge—will cause Ghidra's dead-code elimination passes to completely purge active code sequences.

To bypass the Java UI entirely, cluosh details the programmatic interfaces within libdecomp (specifically the Translate interface, AssemblyEmit, and PcodeEmit). By instantiating a raw loader (LoadImage) that implements loadFill() via memcpy and mapping target binary dumps into memory, a developer can load an .sla file into a Sleigh instance, configure processor context registers, and iterate through address ranges to output disassembled assembly or lift raw P-code directly from the command line.

Key Takeaways:
Reverse engineers can harness Ghidra's native C++ engine (libdecomp and compiled .sla specifications) as standalone, headless libraries for high-performance binary analysis, fuzzing, and custom tool development without Java GUI overhead. Analysts working on embedded and hardware targets must explicitly tag memory-mapped I/O address ranges as volatile and ensure precise function prototypes to prevent Ghidra's optimization passes from erroneously removing valid operations. Finally, examining intermediate P-code via Ghidra's debug XML exports provides crucial visibility into decompiler transformation bugs.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Diogo Lemos & Fábio Pinto - Building vs. Buying - A Tale of Developing an In House SC
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Diogo Lemos & Fábio Pinto - Building vs. Buying - A Tale of Developing an In House SC.
talks.summary:
Build versus buy context

At Balccon, security engineers Diogo and Fabio from Flutter Entertainment and Platy describe choosing to build an in-house software composition analysis platform instead of buying one, unusual for a large organization that typically procures tools.

Why SCA matters

They define SCA as inventorying open-source and third-party dependencies for known vulnerabilities. Modern apps accumulate direct and transitive dependencies via npm, pip, and similar package managers; forgotten libraries persist for years and explode in complexity across thousands of repositories.

Requirements they designed

Their solution needs a dependency inventory mapped to projects and roles, version tracking, continuous CVE synchronization, developer-friendly remediation UX, and ongoing scanning tied to commits and branches. Without automation and good UI, teams ignore massive backlogs.

Developer adoption

They stress that one-click renovate-to-safe-version workflows matter more than raw findings, shifting remediation burden off overwhelmed engineering teams while keeping dependency data fresh as code changes.

talks.title: Direct
talks.teaser: Security researchers investigate Direct and analyze defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Hardware hacker Flo introduces the design, firmware, and architectural trade-offs of the official BalCCon electronic conference badge. Presented at BalCCon, the talk outlines the engineering decisions behind building an ultra-low-cost, hackable RISC-V badge. Flo details the board's microcontroller constraints, analog input multiplexing, inter-badge communication bus, and built-in interactive firmware features developed with contributor Meo.

Key Topics:
- Low-cost embedded engineering using the WCH CH32V003 RISC-V microcontroller
- Programming under tight resource constraints (16 KB Flash, 2 KB SRAM, no malloc)
- Analog input multiplexing using resistor ladders and ADC GPIOs
- Inter-badge communication via I2C, WCH-Link programming, and multiplayer games

Technical Details:
To deliver a free, functional badge to conference attendees while minimizing production costs, Flo selected the WCH CH32V003 microcontroller, an entry-level 32-bit RISC-V core costing approximately ten cents in volume. The microchip presents extreme memory and execution constraints: exactly 16 kilobytes of Flash ROM for executable code and 2 kilobytes of effective SRAM. These limitations completely rule out dynamic memory allocation, meaning standard C `malloc` cannot be used; all data structures, buffers, and state machines must be statically allocated in registers and global RAM. Power is delivered directly from an attached 3V to 5V battery pack without reverse-polarity, over-voltage, or under-voltage protection circuitry to minimize Bill-of-Materials (BOM) cost.

The badge hardware incorporates an ST7735 color LCD display connected via SPI, a piezo buzzer driven by toggling GPIO output frequencies to synthesize square-wave tones, and six tactile buttons split into two 3-button gamepads. To conserve limited microcontroller GPIO pins, the buttons are multiplexed onto two analog-to-digital converter (ADC) pins using resistor ladder networks. Pressing individual buttons or simultaneous combinations alters the circuit resistance, producing distinct analog voltage levels that firmware routines decode into digital input events. The PCB features six edge connectors that route shared power, ground, and I2C communication lines, allowing the badge to draw power and communicate with previous-year BalCCon badges or link multiple badges together in daisy-chained topologies.

The badge firmware ships with two primary interactive applications: a Melody Maker music composer (developed by Meo) allowing users to sequence musical notes, silences, and adjustable BPM speeds, and a fully functional Pong game. Pong can be played in single-player mode, two-player local mode sharing the split gamepad buttons, or multi-device mode where two badges exchange paddle coordinates and ball vectors over an I2C protocol defined in the open-source firmware headers. Firmware flashing is conducted using WCH-Link hardware debuggers via the Rust-based `wlink` CLI tool or custom ESP32 and Raspberry Pi programmer bridges.

Key Takeaways:
Modern RISC-V microcontrollers like the CH32V003 make it feasible to build feature-rich, interactive embedded devices under extreme budget constraints when paired with careful resource management. Developers targeting constrained microcontrollers must utilize static memory allocation and analog multiplexing techniques like resistor ladders to maximize limited pinouts and RAM. Providing open-source schematics, standard I2C expansion headers, and accessible flashing workflows fosters active community engagement and custom firmware experimentation at hardware hacking events.
